html:
From 1885 to 1951 Canadian law banned the potlatch, the great feast and gift giving ceremony of the peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast. It was added to the Indian Act in 1884.

Missionaries and officials saw the potlatch as wasteful and a barrier to Christian conversion. For the peoples of the coast it was the heart of law, rank, marriage and memory.

Many held potlatches in secret. In 1921 police raided a large potlatch held by Dan Cranmer at Village Island, among the Kwakwaka'wakw. Dozens were jailed, and masks and regalia were seized and sold to museums. The ban was quietly dropped in 1951. Some of the treasures were returned from the 1970s and are shown at Alert Bay, a story like that of the residential schools.
sum: From 1885 to 1951 Canadian law banned the potlatch, the great feast and gift giving ceremony of the peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast. It was added to the Indian Act in 1884.
